thread: The contamination is active in living flesh before death

evidence.clue: Deer and wolves run together out of the holly straight at riders; eyes white and filmed like boiled-milk skin; wolves rack-thin with patchy coats coming away, skin grey and scabbed beneath; the wolves hunt silently.

A doe shot through the heart (Sylvanas's arrow) kept running, bled from the nose in two strings, took a neck arrow and kept coming; only a skull shot stopped her. The stag slid on at full stretch with legs still running.
Cyndia: deer slots and wolf pads in the same track, wolf tracks not spread for running; nothing was chasing anything.
Jaina inside the doe: contamination through blood, meat and every organ, liver worst; in the doe long before the arrows.
Horses: the grey's cut and the grey himself read clean ('Hot horse. Tired horse. Clean blood'); Jaina wants to re-check tonight.

Re-check paid in Ch3: all horses, the grey's near-hock tooth-score scabbed black and Sylvanas's mare read 'Clean... Tired horses, nothing else.' Jaina: they have walked through it all day and drunk at the culvert stream; she does not understand why they are clean.

A man's clog standing upright in the lane, the prints after it bare; Sylvanas: 'The doe had not cared either. She had come on with a split heart, alive when she ran. Were these alive when they walked?' She forbids herself equating them ('Don't make them into the doe').
In the girl's account sweetness of breath ('pears gone brown') preceded fever; a symptom reported by a child, not a mechanism. Sylvanas thinks of a drunk's or a dying man's sweet breath.
Jaina wants 'one of them' to test whether the dead were alive when they walked (not available). Prints are heavier than the ground, as the doe was.
The barn cat is plainly ordinary (clean coat, well-fed). The rooks in the stubble (Ch2) and the cat suggest not all animals are affected; no pattern asserted.

Chapter 4: the contamination is in living HUMANS before death. Early cases: a fist or less under the breastbone, a thread along the gut, nothing in blood, lungs, arms or head; late case (Garran): in liver, lungs, great vessels, down both arms to the fingers, all threads running back to the gut. It is physical and cumulative with dose. Jaina recalls the doe ('roots in a pot') and has 'not seen it in a man who was still breathing'.
Chapter 4: Tam, who guarded the jar but never ate the flour, reads clean in the gut after death; the contamination does not simply 'take' anyone nearby: it has to be swallowed.
Chapter 4: Jaina holds the drag in the sick with the holding ward (it stops it going further, cannot clear it): early cases improve (Elsie's fever breaks) once the dose stops.

readerKnows: The contamination is in the living animals, in Millhaven's water and ground, in the footprints of the dead; horses and the cat read or look clean; people in Millhaven fell sick, died, rose and walked out.
povCharacterKnows: Sylvanas: she has the doe, the sweet-breath symptom and the dead's walking as separate facts and refuses to equate them. Jaina: how it sits in the tissue and ground; not the mechanism, not the entry route.
notes_chapter4: SUPERSEDES the Ch3 caution: the entry route is now established (swallowed, in flour). The mechanism that raises the dead is still unknown. Whether the doe and horses (clean) fit the flour model is unexplained: horses eat oats and hay not the new flour; the doe's route is unknown.
notes: [Chapter 3 note, now superseded by chapter 4] Do not name grain as carrier. The entry method is explicitly unknown. Horses are clean as of the night re-check. Sweet breath is a symptom, not a mechanism.
